pages.text:
*Way to Lose #16: Write down one true thing about yourself, then cross it out because it's not about soccer.*

The field at Marigold Park is a swamp. The rain hasn't stopped in two days, and the grass looks like it has given up on being grass. So we are at the bus depot, standing in the cracked asphalt between the idling yellow buses. The air smells like diesel and hot rubber. It is loud. A bus engine shudders to life behind me, and I flinch.

Coach Gin stands in front of us, her fluorescent windbreaker zipped to her chin. She holds a stack of white index cards. They are crisp. They have never been used.

“Write one true thing about yourself,” she says. Her voice cuts through the engine noise. “A thing that a scoreboard cannot change. A thing that does not depend on the score. Fold it. Put it in your sock.”

I look at the card. It is blank. It is terrifying. I take a pencil. My hand hovers over the paper. The bus engine sputters again, and the vibration travels through the soles of my cleats.
pages.image: A group of young soccer players stand on cracked asphalt between parked big blank yellow minibus; a short woman in a bright yellow windbreaker holds a stack of white cards, and a girl in a red jersey looks nervous near an idling engine.

pages.text:
Tank goes first. The small card looks like a ticket stub in his huge hands. He writes, “I can make a decent croissant.” He folds it carefully and tucks it into his right sock. He looks pleased.

Josie writes, “I notice everything.” She does not fold it. She just shoves it into her pocket. Ollie smiles and adds, “I remember everybody’s birthday.” He is already humming a tune.

The twins, Leo and Mateo, pass a single card back and forth. They both write, “We are the best at arguing.” Their handwriting is identical, which is weird, because they are supposed to be different.

Priya writes something. She scrubs it with her eraser. She writes it again. She folds the card so tight it cracks. She hides it inside her glove, under the thick padding. No one sees it.

Ahmed writes, “I’m fast.”

Gin reads it over his shoulder. She does not blink.

“Fast is a fact,” she says. “Try again.”
pages.image: A large boy gently places a small card into his sock; a girl in goalie gloves hides a card inside her gear; a lanky boy looks frustrated as a woman in sunglasses reads his small piece of paper.

pages.text:
I have held my pencil for eleven minutes, counting the seconds, the idling engines, and the lines on the card.

I think about soccer. I am good at passing, or at least I am when the ball reaches my teammate, when they do not drop it, and when we happen to win. It feels less like a skill and more like a gamble.

I think about being fast, which is just a fact, like Ahmed, and not a person.

I think about being captain. I write the word. CAPTAIN. The letters are jagged. I hate them. Nobody voted. It just happened, the way a bruise happens. It is a title given to me by a team that cannot stop the other team from scoring.

I cross it out, and the pencil snaps. A chunk of graphite shatters on the asphalt. I stare at the broken tip. I stare at the blank space where the truth should be.

I do not have a truth. I have a record. And my record is a hole in the ground that keeps getting deeper.
pages.image: A girl with a high ponytail and a yellow armband holds a snapped pencil over a white card on her knee; she looks distressed as she stares at the broken graphite tip and the blank paper.

pages.text:
Gin walks over. She does not ask what is wrong. She looks at the card, then at the blank space.

“Is that true when you lose?” she asks.

I open my mouth, but nothing comes out. My throat feels packed with dry autumn leaves.

My dad walks out from between the buses, wearing his mechanic’s shirt stained with grease. He waves at the team, then spots me.

“Hey, Dani!” he hollers. “Check your laces. One is green, one is orange. It’s a mess. You look like a broken traffic light.”

I laugh. It is a small, dry sound.

Dad stands beside me. He looks at the card. He does not ask what I wrote. He does not ask how I feel. He has never asked how I feel. He asks about the score. He asks about the standings.

I realize I have never told him that the score is the only thing that makes me feel real. I realize he thinks I am fine. I am not fine. I am empty.
pages.image: A man in a greasy mechanic's shirt waves cheerfully at a group of kids; he stands next to a girl in a red jersey who looks anxious; a woman in a yellow jacket watches them from a short distance.

pages.text:
The practice ends, and the drills blur into a repetitive haze of passing and running. The ball hits the asphalt, bouncing up with that hard, unpredictable snap that makes your feet flinch.

I take off my right cleat, peel out the sock, and unfold the card. It is still blank. It is still a question waiting to be answered.

I fold it carefully, then fold it again until it is small enough to fit in my palm. It feels sharp, like a piece of paper cut from a test I failed.

I put it back in the sock and pull it up. The card sits under my ankle bone, scratchy and warm, a secret weight against my skin.

I lace up my cleat, tying the green lace tight, then the orange one. As I stand, the bus engine roars to life, and the vibration hums through my legs like a low-frequency hum.

I am ready for the next drill. The card is still there, waiting.
pages.image: A close-up of a girl's foot as she tucks a small folded card into her white sock; she is wearing a cleat with one green and one orange lace, standing on gray asphalt near a big blank yellow minibus tire.
